common_name: Starlite Prairieblues Baptisia (Pale Blue-Violet False Indigo Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall into deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Starlite Prairieblues is a Chicago Botanic Garden hybrid bred alongside Twilite Prairieblues and Solar Flare, combining native Baptisia parentage into a more floriferous garden plant.

directions: Plant container-grown plants in spring or fall in deep, well-drained soil in full sun, siting Starlite Prairieblues in its permanent spot from the start since its deep taproot resents disturbance once established. This Chicago Botanic Garden hybrid opens in soft blue-violet tones that pale toward the edge of each floret, giving the spikes an icy, luminous cast distinct from the deeper violet-purple of its Twilite Prairieblues sibling, and it flowers on sturdy, upright stems above blue-green foliage in late spring. Like other Prairieblues introductions it pairs native Baptisia toughness with a fuller, more floriferous habit than the wild species, followed by dark seed pods that add texture into fall and winter. Established clumps are extremely drought-tolerant, long-lived, and essentially maintenance-free, needing only an occasional late-winter cutback.

common_name: Decadence Sparkling Sapphires Baptisia (Compact Violet-Blue False Indigo)

planting.note: Plant container plants in spring in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and resents transplanting once established; Sparkling Sapphires is a compact Decadence-series hybrid with rich violet-blue flowers on an upright, tidy form.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average soil in full sun to light partial shade, choosing a permanent site since Baptisia develops a deep taproot and does not transplant well once established. Sparkling Sapphires is a compact Decadence-series hybrid bearing dense spikes of rich violet-blue, pea-like flowers more saturated than the species-blue of Baptisia australis, on an upright, tidy plant scaled for smaller borders than the sprawling wild species. Following bloom, dark seedpods provide fall and winter interest, and the plant serves as a larval host for several native butterfly species while its flowers draw bumblebees. It is extremely drought-tolerant and essentially maintenance-free once established, functioning almost like a small flowering shrub; avoid dividing or transplanting mature plants, simply cutting back in late winter if a tidier form is wanted.

planting.note: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun around the last frost date; Alba is a long-grown, simple white-flowered selection of dense blazing star distinct from the taller Floristan White introduction.

directions: Plant corms 2 to 3 inches deep in moist, well-drained soil in full sun in mid-spring once hard frost danger has passed. Alba is a long-grown, simple white-flowered selection of dense blazing star, producing the same tall, densely packed bottlebrush spikes as the species but in clean white rather than magenta-purple, opening from the top of the spike downward as is typical of the genus. Its grassy summer foliage and upright habit combine well with ornamental grasses and other late-summer perennials, and the flowers draw butterflies and bees while goldfinches feed on the ripened seed if spikes are left standing into winter. Clumps multiply steadily from year to year and benefit from division every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and prevent overcrowding.
